notes: Permission-to-appeal judgment on residence transfer and costs; substantive appeal refused but costs appeal granted.

enrichment.short_title: Re T: permission to appeal residence transfer and children costs order
key_facts: JT, aged five, was the subject of prolonged contact and residence litigation between his parents ST and DT after their 2002 separation.
Judge Kushner had dismissed domestic violence and sexual abuse allegations in January 2003, but contact broke down and in February 2004 transferred residence from the mother to the father.
In June 2004 the judge ordered the mother to pay about £15,000 plus other costs of the children proceedings, finding her conduct unreasonable though linked to anxiety and belief in abuse.
By the permission hearing the parents had achieved an informal 60/40 shared arrangement and the child had settled.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal two county court decisions on residence and costs before Mrs Justice Black.
enrichment.outcome: Permission refused on the residence transfer because there was no real prospect of success; permission granted on the costs issue only, to be heard by two Lords Justices.
enrichment.ratio: A transfer of residence based on welfare findings about a parent's inability to promote contact may be tenable even where a CAFCASS officer did not recommend it, provided reasons are given; costs orders in children proceedings remain exceptional and a judge who found the mother's unreasonableness stemmed from personality, belief and welfare concern may have misapplied the discretion.
legal_issues: Whether Judge Kushner erred in transferring residence to the father
Whether remaining sexual abuse concerns could be taken into account after a finding of fact
Whether additional psychological assessment was required
Whether a costs order was a proper exercise of discretion in children proceedings

confidence.notes: Dispositions on permission and the split outcome on residence versus costs are clearly stated.

notes: Section 204 housing appeal; Laws LJ restored the review decision on vulnerability and fact-finding limits.

enrichment.short_title: Enfield v Kruja: priority need and section 204 housing appeal
key_facts: The Kruja family, Kosovan nationals granted asylum, applied to Enfield as homeless in April 2003.
The council found them homeless but not in priority need, relying on medical and mental health panel advice about PTSD and depression.
On section 204 appeal Judge Cotran held the review decision Wednesbury unreasonable and quashed it.
Psychiatric evidence included Dr Blaj's report that Dritan Kruja did not suffer from mental illness, alongside later severe PTSD diagnoses.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Local housing authority appeal with permission against a county court decision allowing a section 204 appeal and quashing a section 202 review.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the county court had usurped the authority's fact-finding role and the review panel had correctly applied the Pereira vulnerability test.
enrichment.ratio: On a section 204 appeal the county court conducts statutory judicial review only; it cannot treat conflicting psychiatric evidence as all one way or substitute its own finding of mental illness where Dr Blaj's report supported the authority's conclusion and the review panel directed itself according to Pereira.
legal_issues: Whether the county court exceeded its section 204 jurisdiction
Whether Dritan Kruja suffered mental illness for section 189(1)(c) purposes
Whether the family was less able to fend for itself than an ordinary homeless person
Application of the Pereira vulnerability test
linked_authorities: R v Brent LBC ex parte Pereira [1998] 31 HLR 317
Nipa Begum v Tower Hamlets LBC [2000] 1 WLR 306

confidence.notes: Statutory framework, appellate reasoning and restoration of the review decision are explicit.

notes: ASBO sentencing judicial review; Crown Court decision quashed but sentence substituted because claimant had served equivalent time.

enrichment.short_title: R (K) v Newport Crown Court: irrational disparity in youth ASBO sentences
key_facts: A 16-year-old claimant was sentenced to 12 months' detention and training for breaching a final ASBO and four months consecutive for handbag theft, totalling 16 months.
Co-defendant A received four months for ASBO breaches despite earlier interim ASBO breaches and prior custody.
The Newport Crown Court dismissed the sentence appeal with brief, partly inaudible reasons citing a difference between the defendants.
By the judicial review hearing the claimant had been in custody since 28 April and had effectively served a 12-month DTO.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Crown Court's dismissal of an appeal against magistrates' sentences for ASBO breach and theft.
enrichment.outcome: Crown Court decision quashed as irrational on the papers, but rather than remit the court substituted a total 12-month sentence (eight months ASBO, four months theft) because of delay and time already served.
enrichment.ratio: Where two young defendants sentenced together receive markedly disparate ASBO custodial terms and neither magistrates nor Crown Court adequately explain the disparity on the available material, the McGeary/Sogbesan test for quashing a Crown Court sentencing decision is satisfied; inadequate pre-sentence information and reasons may vitiate the appeal decision.
legal_issues: Whether the Crown Court's reasons supported the sentencing disparity
Application of R v DPP ex parte McGeary and R (Sogbesan)
Whether the matter should be remitted or a substituted sentence imposed
Adequacy of information before magistrates and Crown Court on ASBO breaches
linked_authorities: R v Director of Public Prosecutions ex parte McGeary (1999) 2 Cr App R (S) 263
R (Sogbesan) v Inner London Crown Court (2003) 1 Cr App R (S) 79

confidence.notes: Outcome and substituted sentence are clear though underlying sentencing merits were not finally determined.

notes: Disability Discrimination Act appeal on Thetford station access; cost concession shaped the reasonableness finding.

enrichment.short_title: Roads v Central Trains: DDA reasonable adjustment at Thetford station
key_facts: Mr Roads, a wheelchair user from Norwich, could not safely use the footbridge or Station Lane route to reach platform 1 at Thetford.
Central Trains offered free travel via Ely as an alternative, adding over an hour to a 36-minute journey.
The claimant sought provision of a wheelchair-accessible taxi from Norwich with adequate notice; the operator conceded cost was not in issue at trial.
The county court held it was not reasonable to require the taxi solution.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from dismissal of a Disability Discrimination Act claim for failure to make reasonable adjustments to inter-platform access.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; judgment entered for £1,097 damages because, on the agreed cost-free assumption and with notice, requiring the Ely detour was not a reasonable alternative method under section 21(2)(d).
enrichment.ratio: Section 21(2) requires consideration of whether a physical feature makes access impossible or unreasonably difficult for disabled persons of the relevant kind before asking what steps are reasonable; where a better practicable alternative exists and cost has been excluded from the balance, directing a wheelchair user on a lengthy detour rather than a short taxi transfer fails the DDA policy of approximating ordinary access.
legal_issues: Whether access between platforms was part of the service provided
Whether Station Lane was unreasonably difficult for wheelchair users
Whether the Ely route was a reasonable alternative method of access
Effect of the operator's concession excluding taxi cost from reasonableness
linked_authorities: In re Holy Cross, Pershore [2002] Fam 1

confidence.notes: Detailed DDA analysis and allowance of appeal are clear, though the court emphasised the case turned on unusual assumed facts.

notes: VAT zero-rating appeal on charity day nursery; tribunal decision upheld following Yarburgh.

enrichment.short_title: Customs & Excise v St Paul's: VAT zero-rating of charity nursery building works
key_facts: St Paul's, a Balsall Heath charity, ran a break-even day nursery charging fees below commercial rates and relying heavily on grants including Sure Start.
Construction of a new building including the nursery was zero-rated by the VAT tribunal as use otherwise than in the course of a business under Note (6) to Group 5.
Customs contended the nursery was a business activity because parents paid fees and the operation resembled commercial nurseries.
The nursery admissions policy prioritised local disadvantaged families and staffing exceeded OFSTED minima.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal under section 11 of the Tribunals and Inquiries Act 1992 against a VAT tribunal decision allowing zero-rating of construction works.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the tribunal's conclusion that the nursery was not a business within Note (6)(a) was not perverse and followed Yarburgh.
enrichment.ratio: Business in Note (6)(a) must be given the same meaning as economic activity under Article 4 of the Sixth Directive; payment of fees alone does not determine business status, and a not-for-profit charitable nursery breaking even on concessionary fees may not be predominantly concerned with making taxable supplies for consideration.
legal_issues: Whether the nursery constituted use in the course or furtherance of a business
Whether business and charitable activity were wrongly treated as mutually exclusive
Whether the tribunal was bound by Customs v Yarburgh Children's Trust
Whether the tribunal's factual conclusion was perverse under Edwards v Bairstow
linked_authorities: Customs & Excise Commissioners v Yarburgh Children's Trust [2002] STC 207
Customs & Excise Commissioners v Morrison's Academy Boarding Houses Association [1978] STC 1
Edwards v Bairstow [1956] AC 14

confidence.notes: Long judgment but final dismissal and Yarburgh-based reasoning are clearly expressed.

notes: Landmark post-HRA judgment affirming Bonnard v Perryman in defamation prior restraint applications.

enrichment.short_title: Greene v Associated Newspapers: prior restraint and Bonnard v Perryman after HRA
key_facts: Martha Greene sought to restrain The Mail on Sunday from publishing further articles linking her to convicted fraudster Peter Foster and disputed emails.
Fulford J refused a permanent injunction under Bonnard v Perryman but granted a temporary injunction pending appeal.
The claimant argued Cream Holdings and section 12(3) required a 'more likely than not' test rather than the Bonnard rule.
New computer expert evidence on appeal did not establish it was clear the disputed emails were forgeries.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from refusal of interim injunction restraining publication of an allegedly defamatory article pending libel trial.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the rule in Bonnard v Perryman survived the Human Rights Act and section 12(3) did not relax the prior restraint standard in defamation.
enrichment.ratio: In defamation a court will not restrain publication before trial unless it is clear the defendant's plea of justification must fail; section 12(3) was enacted to protect media freedom in privacy/confidentiality cases and does not by implication abrogate Bonnard, and Article 8 reputation rights do not justify a lower threshold where truth is for trial.
legal_issues: Whether section 12(3) replaced the Bonnard v Perryman test in libel
Whether Article 8 required balancing against Article 10 at the interlocutory stage
Whether the disputed Foster emails were probably forgeries
Relationship between Cream Holdings and defamation prior restraint
linked_authorities: Bonnard v Perryman [1891] 2 Ch 269
Cream Holdings Ltd v Banerjee [2004] UKHL 44
Holley v Smyth [1998] QB 726

confidence.notes: Full appellate judgment on law and fact with clear dismissal of the appeal.

notes: Tobacco POS advertising regulations upheld on proportionality and EU law grounds.

enrichment.short_title: BAT v Secretary of State: challenge to tobacco point-of-sale advertising regulations
key_facts: The 2002 Act banned tobacco advertising subject to a regulated exception for point-of-sale advertisements.
The 2004 Regulations limited POS adverts to one A5 fixed gantry advert with a 30% health warning and restricted vending machine advertising.
Six tobacco industry claimants challenged the Regulations as disproportionate under Article 10 and as discriminatory under EU law.
The Secretary of State relied on the serious health harms of smoking and the strict primary legislation context.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Tobacco Advertising and Promotion (Point of Sale) Regulations 2004 made under section 4(3) of the 2002 Act.
enrichment.outcome: Claim refused; the Regulations were a proportionate restriction on commercial expression in the context of a near-total statutory advertising ban and legitimate public health aims.
enrichment.ratio: Where Parliament has enacted a strict tobacco advertising ban and delegated limited POS exceptions, courts owe deference in reviewing subordinate legislation restricting commercial speech to protect health; A5 gantry adverts, product displays and price lists can still convey meaningful product information and the Regulations were not so restrictive as to impair the essence of commercial free speech.
legal_issues: Whether the Regulations were disproportionate under Article 10
Whether the Regulations were too blunt an instrument focused only on protecting children
Whether Article 28 EC Treaty was infringed against foreign manufacturers
Whether the Minister adequately assessed less severe alternatives
linked_authorities: R (Daly) v Secretary of State [2001] 2 AC 532
R v Shayler [2003] 1 AC 247
Virginia State Board of Pharmacy v Virginia Citizens Consumer Council (1976) 425 US 748

confidence.notes: Comprehensive judgment with clear refusal of all principal grounds of challenge.

notes: Gorringe applied to reject common law duty to salt icy trunk roads after Goodes.

enrichment.short_title: Sandhar v DETR: no common law duty to grit trunk roads for ice
key_facts: Mr Sandhar died when his car skidded on hoar frost on the A428 in Bedfordshire on 22 December 1996.
Bedfordshire County Council under a trunk-road delegation failed to salt after inadequate monitoring by the duty engineer Mr Chandler.
At the time authorities understood section 41 imposed a duty to prevent ice, later overturned in Goodes v East Sussex.
A public pamphlet advised drivers never to assume a road had been salted.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from dismissal of a negligence claim against the Secretary of State after Goodes and Gorringe.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no common law duty of care arose from the winter maintenance scheme because the deceased could not rely on salting and the authority had not assumed responsibility or created a trap.
enrichment.ratio: Following Gorringe, a highway authority's statutory power to improve or grit roads does not without more create a private law duty to prevent ice; motorists remain primarily responsible for their safety, general public expectation of salting is insufficient, and a pamphlet expressly warning drivers not to assume salting negates reliance.
legal_issues: Whether a common law duty existed to salt roads in icy conditions
Effect of Goodes on maintenance duties under section 41
Whether the winter maintenance programme created assumption of responsibility
Whether the authority created a trap by fostering expectation of salting
linked_authorities: Goodes v East Sussex County Council [2000] 1 WLR 1356
Gorringe v Calderdale MBC [2004] UKHL 15
Stovin v Wise [1996] AC 923

confidence.notes: Central legal issue and dismissal after Gorringe are comprehensively reasoned.

notes: Section 423 vesting order appeal; matrimonial creditor cannot jump bankruptcy queue via s423.

enrichment.short_title: Ram v Ram: section 423 vesting and matrimonial claims in bankruptcy
key_facts: Baskinder Ram was made bankrupt in 1998 owing substantial tax and other debts.
He had transferred a quarter-share in 11 Westfield Road to relatives at an undervalue in 1996 to defeat creditors.
His wife obtained a section 423 order setting aside the transfer but sought re-vesting in the husband rather than the trustee.
Matrimonial proceedings produced orders for transfer of the home and a £150,000 lump sum, but family orders are not provable in bankruptcy under rule 12.3.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against a judge's order vesting the recovered quarter-share in the trustee in bankruptcy under section 423.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; vesting in the trustee restored the pre-transaction position and protected victims without giving the wife priority over bankruptcy creditors.
enrichment.ratio: Section 423(2) requires conjunctive restoration of the debtor's position and protection of victims; property recovered from a transaction defrauding creditors belongs in the bankrupt's estate for the trustee unless special circumstances apply, and rule 12.3's exclusion of family orders from proof cannot be circumvented by vesting assets outside the bankruptcy.
legal_issues: Proper form of section 423 order where wife and creditors are both victims
Whether the wife could be re-vested with property to pursue matrimonial claims
Whether rule 12.3 discriminates against matrimonial creditors under Article 14
Interaction of section 423 with bankruptcy administration
linked_authorities: Chohan v Saggar [1994] 1 BCLC 706
Woodley v Woodley (No 2) [1994] 1 WLR 1167
Re Mordant [1996] 1 FLR 334

confidence.notes: Statutory construction and dismissal on insolvency and Convention grounds are clearly reasoned.

notes: Planning permission quashed for false owner certificates and mandatory notice breaches.

enrichment.short_title: Pridmore v Salisbury: quashing planning permission for owner-notice failures

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (General Development Procedure) Order 1995

key_facts: Mr Docking applied to build a bungalow at the rear of 38 Firs Road, Salisbury, with driveway access affecting neighbours' land.
He submitted false ownership certificates and never served the Pridmores as owners before or after amending the plans.
The council processed the application under an erroneous eight-week deadline assumption and granted permission on 27 February 2004.
Amended plans were not referred to the Highway Authority and gave inadequate time for representations on turning and access issues.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Salisbury District Council's grant of planning permission after permission hearing combined with substantive hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted and claim allowed; planning permission quashed because mandatory owner-notification requirements were breached and discretion under Main v Swansea required quashing.
enrichment.ratio: Owner notification and certificate requirements under the GDPO are mandatory; where an applicant knowingly submits false certificates, the authority entertains an invalid application, and neighbours-as-owners receive no valid notice, a grant of permission is voidable and should be quashed especially where prejudice to turning and highway access could have differed with proper consultation.
legal_issues: Whether owner notification requirements were mandatory
Exercise of discretion to quash under Main v Swansea City Council
Whether neighbours received adequate time to object to amended plans
Failure to consult the Highway Authority on amended access
linked_authorities: Main v Swansea City Council (1984) 49 P & CR 26

confidence.notes: Detailed chronology of procedural defects and quashing on the principal ground are explicit.
